newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU probes cost of telecoms leased lines.
newsitem.headline: EU probes cost of telecoms leased lines.

text.p: The European Commission is investigating complaints that Europe's big telephone companies are overcharging customers for leased telecommunications lines.

The European Union executive is studying data provided by the International Telecommunications Users Group (INTUG) showing huge differences between charges for national and international lines, a Commission official said.
The group also found big variations in prices charged for analog and digital lines.
EU rules require phone companies to base charges for leased lines on actual costs, which means international lines should not subsidise local ones.

INTUG, an organisation with headquarters in Namur, Belgium, that groups multinational corporations and other big telecoms users, compared prices charged by dominant phone operators in 12 European countries.

It found that customers leasing lines to build an international network -- for example companies wanting to link its subsidiaries -- were paying up to 5.5 times more than they would pay for national lines covering the same distance.

"The differences are very big," the Commission official said. "There can be all kinds of reasons for that, but then it's up to national regulatory authorities to examine whether the cost base of these tariffs is justified or not."
He said the Commission had referred the issue to a committee of national authorities that meets the Commission to discuss EU legislation covering access to phone networks.
While the first step is up to EU governments, the Commission could threaten action before the European Court of Justice if they failed to stem any illegal charging practices, he said.

The INTUG report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, shows that the biggest variation between international and domestic lines is in Denmark. The monthly price charged there last August for a digital two-megabit line was 548 percent more than for a similar national line.
A similar international line in Britain cost 467 percent more than a national one, it shows.

The differences between digital and analog lines were even more pronounced. The price for an 80-km digital two-megabit line in Belgium was a whopping 3,048 percent higher than an analog line running the same distance.
Dominant phone operators such as TeleDanmark A/S, France Telecom and Deutsche Telecom have justified higher international costs on various grounds, according to a summary provided by INTUG.

They argue, for example, that the volume of international circuits leased is much lower than national ones so they cannot profit from economies of scale and that they bear costs related to dealing with phone companies in other countries to connect networks.
TeleDanmark also argued that it bore the cost of laying submarine cables.
